questions.q: An $\alpha$-helix is a structural feature of :
questions.solution:
The $\alpha$-helix is a form of the **secondary structure of proteins** — the way a polypeptide chain coils up locally.

In it, the chain winds into a right-handed spiral held in place by **intramolecular hydrogen bonds** between the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ of one amino acid residue and the $\text{N}-\text{H}$ of the residue four places along the chain.

Checking the others:

- **Sucrose** is a disaccharide — a single small molecule of glucose and fructose, with no chain to coil.
- **Starch** is a polysaccharide; amylose does form a helix, but it is held by a different arrangement and the $\alpha$-helix specifically names the protein structure.
- **Nucleotides** are the individual building blocks of nucleic acids; DNA's structure is a **double helix**, and that is a different thing again.

So the $\alpha$-helix belongs to **polypeptides**.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-reducing sugar?
questions.solution:
**Sucrose** is non-reducing: the glycosidic link joins glucose's C1 to fructose's C2, so neither anomeric carbon is free to open into a carbonyl.

Maltose and lactose keep one free anomeric carbon and **are** reducing. Fructose, though a ketose, is reducing too, because in alkali it isomerises to an aldose.

questions.q: The bond joining two amino acids in a protein is:
questions.solution:
A **peptide bond** ($-\text{CO–NH}-$), formed by condensation between one amino acid's carboxyl group and the next one's amino group, losing water.

It has partial double-bond character, so it is planar and rigid — which is exactly what makes the $\alpha$-helix and $\beta$-sheet possible.

questions.q: Denaturation of a protein destroys its:
questions.solution:
Heat, acid or heavy metals break the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the chain's **shape**, so the secondary and tertiary structure is lost.

The **primary structure** — the sequence, held by covalent peptide bonds — survives.

Boiling an egg is denaturation: the same molecules, permanently rearranged, and no amount of cooling puts them back.

questions.q: The sugar present in RNA is:
questions.solution:
RNA contains **ribose**; DNA contains 2-deoxyribose, which lacks the oxygen at C2.

That missing $-\text{OH}$ is why DNA is chemically far more stable — and so the right molecule for storing information long-term, while RNA does the short-lived work.

questions.q: How many naturally occurring amino acids are found in proteins?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{20}$ standard amino acids, of which about ten are **essential** — the human body cannot make them and they must come from food.

All twenty share the same backbone and differ only in the side chain $-\text{R}$.

questions.q: How many peptide bonds are present in a linear tripeptide?
questions.solution:
A chain of $n$ amino acids has $n - 1$ peptide bonds, so a tripeptide has $\mathbf{2}$.

Like fence posts and the panels between them.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of glucose, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$, in g/mol. (C $= 12$, H $= 1$, O $= 16$.)
How many chiral carbon atoms does glucose have in its open-chain form?
questions.solution:
Carbons 2, 3, 4 and 5 each carry four different groups — $\mathbf{4}$ chiral centres.

That gives $2^{4} = 16$ possible stereoisomers, of which D-glucose is one. (In the cyclic form C1 also becomes chiral, producing the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ anomers.)

questions.q: In a DNA double helix, adenine pairs with thymine through how many hydrogen bonds?
questions.solution:
A–T pair with **2** hydrogen bonds; G–C with 3.

This is why DNA rich in G–C needs a higher temperature to separate the strands — three ties are harder to undo than two.

questions.q: Give the evidence for the open-chain structure of glucose, and explain why a cyclic structure had to be proposed.
questions.solution:
**Evidence for the open chain.**

1. **Molecular formula** $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$; on prolonged heating with HI it gives **n-hexane**, so all six carbons are in a straight chain.

2. **Reacts with hydroxylamine** to give an oxime and adds HCN to give a cyanohydrin — so a **carbonyl** group is present.

3. **Reduces Tollens' and Fehling's** and is oxidised by bromine water to gluconic acid — so it is an **aldehyde**, not a ketone.

4. **Acetylation with acetic anhydride gives a penta-acetate** — so there are **five $-\text{OH}$ groups**, one on each of the other carbons.

5. **Nitric acid oxidation gives saccharic acid**, a dicarboxylic acid — so there is a primary alcohol at the far end.

**Why the open chain is not enough.**

1. Glucose does **not** give the Schiff's test, and does not form a bisulphite addition compound — behaviour unlike a normal aldehyde.

2. The pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine, implying no free $-\text{CHO}$.

3. Glucose exists as **two crystalline forms**, $\alpha$ ($110°$C, $+111°$ rotation) and $\beta$ ($150°$C, $+19.2°$), which in solution slowly converge to $+52.5°$ — **mutarotation**.

**Resolution.** Glucose is mainly a **six-membered cyclic hemiacetal** (pyranose), formed when the C5 hydroxyl adds to the C1 aldehyde. C1 becomes chiral, giving the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ anomers, and mutarotation is the two forms equilibrating through a trace of the open chain.

questions.q: Describe the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures of proteins.
questions.solution:
**Primary.** The **sequence** of amino acids in the chain, held by covalent peptide bonds. Change one residue and the whole protein may fail — sickle-cell anaemia is a single substitution in haemoglobin.

**Secondary.** The local folding of the backbone, held by **hydrogen bonds** between the C=O and N–H groups:

• **$\alpha$-helix** — a right-handed coil, hydrogen bonded within the chain (keratin in hair and wool).

• **$\beta$-pleated sheet** — extended chains hydrogen bonded side by side (silk fibroin).

**Tertiary.** The overall three-dimensional shape of one chain, held by hydrogen bonds, disulphide bridges, ionic bonds and **hydrophobic interactions** — the last of which drive non-polar side chains into the interior, away from water.

This is the level that creates an enzyme's active site, and so the level on which function depends.

**Quaternary.** The arrangement of **two or more chains** into one functional unit. Haemoglobin is four subunits, and its ability to bind oxygen cooperatively exists only because of that arrangement.

**Fibrous proteins** (keratin, collagen) are long, insoluble and structural; **globular proteins** (haemoglobin, enzymes, insulin) are folded, soluble and functional.

questions.q: Classify vitamins and give the deficiency disease of four of them. Then state the two differences between DNA and RNA and the function of each.
questions.solution:
**Vitamins** fall into two classes:

• **Fat soluble** — A, D, E, K. Stored in the liver and fatty tissue, so an overdose is possible.

• **Water soluble** — the B group and C. Not stored (except $\text{B}_{12}$), so they must be supplied regularly.

**Deficiency diseases:**

• **A** — xerophthalmia, night blindness

• **$\text{B}_{1}$** — beri-beri

• **C** — scurvy

• **D** — rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults

• **K** — poor blood clotting

**DNA against RNA:**

1. **Sugar:** DNA has 2-deoxyribose; RNA has ribose.

2. **Bases:** DNA uses thymine; RNA uses uracil in its place. Both use adenine, guanine and cytosine.

3. **Structure:** DNA is a double helix; RNA is usually single-stranded.

**Functions.** DNA stores the hereditary information and replicates it. RNA carries out its instructions: messenger RNA copies the message, transfer RNA brings the amino acids, ribosomal RNA is part of the machine that joins them.

The missing $-\text{OH}$ at C2 makes DNA much the more stable of the two, which is exactly what an archive needs and a working copy does not.

questions.q: What are enzymes? Describe their characteristics and mechanism of action.
questions.solution:
**What they are.** Biological catalysts, almost all of them globular proteins, that speed up the reactions of living systems — often by a factor of $10^{6}$ to $10^{12}$.

**Characteristics.**

1. **Highly specific** — one enzyme, usually one substrate. Maltase acts on maltose and on nothing else.

2. **Efficient** at very low concentration.

3. **Work under mild conditions** — body temperature, near-neutral pH, atmospheric pressure. Compare the Haber process, which needs $700$ K and $200$ atm to do something nitrogen-fixing bacteria manage in soil.

4. **Sensitive** to temperature and pH, because both denature the protein. Each has an optimum.

**Mechanism.**

**Step 1.** The substrate binds at the **active site**, a pocket whose shape and chemistry fit it — the *lock and key* picture, refined into *induced fit*, in which the enzyme closes round the substrate.

**Step 2.** The enzyme–substrate complex reacts. The enzyme holds the substrate in the right orientation, strains the bond to be broken, and offers acidic or basic groups — **lowering the activation energy**.

**Step 3.** The product leaves and the enzyme is free to start again, unchanged.

An enzyme changes the **rate**, never the position of equilibrium.

questions.q: What are zwitterions? Explain why amino acids are high-melting solids and why they have an isoelectric point.
questions.solution:
**Zwitterion.** An amino acid does not exist as $\text{H}_{2}\text{N–CHR–COOH}$. The carboxyl group is acidic and the amino group basic, so the proton transfers internally:

$\text{H}_{3}\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{–CHR–COO}^{-}$

The molecule is **internally ionised** while remaining overall neutral.

**Why they are high-melting solids.** Being ionic, they form a crystal held by strong electrostatic forces, so they melt high (often with decomposition, above $200$°C) — quite unlike comparable amines or acids, which are liquids. They are soluble in water and nearly insoluble in organic solvents, for the same reason.

**Isoelectric point.** In acid, the zwitterion takes another proton and becomes a **cation**; in alkali it loses one and becomes an **anion**.

At one particular pH — the **isoelectric point** — the two forms exactly balance and the molecule carries **no net charge**. There it does not migrate in an electric field, and its solubility is at a minimum.

That is precisely what makes **electrophoresis** work: at a chosen pH, different amino acids carry different charges and travel at different speeds, so a mixture separates.
